chapters.title: Chapter 4: Does Sector Rotation Actually Work in India?

lessons.title: Testing the Clock: Nifty Sectoral Index Returns Across Indian Cycles

body.text: A model you never test is just a story. This lesson puts the sector rotation clock against actual NSE index returns across India's recent cycles, and the result is more useful than a simple yes or no.

children.text: Chapter 3 built the textbook version of sector rotation: rate sensitives lead the recovery, capex and commodity sectors lead the mid and late cycle, and defensives protect in a slowdown. Those patterns came mostly from US studies. Here we test them on Nifty sectoral index data, year by year, from 2018 to September 2026, a period that includes a slowdown, a contraction, a recovery, a hiking cycle, an easing cycle, and a crude oil shock.
The Data and the Method

Every number in this lesson is calculated from the official closing values of NSE indices on the last trading day of each year, taken from NSE's daily index files, with 2026 measured to the close on 15 September 2026. The method is deliberately simple, so you can repeat it yourself.

body.latex: \text{Relative return (pp)} = R_{\text{sector}} - R_{\text{Nifty 50}} \qquad R_{\text{2 years}} = (1 + R_1)(1 + R_2) - 1
body.caption: Relative return in percentage points (pp) shows whether a sector beat or lagged the market; multi-year returns are compounded, not added

children.text: Step 1: label each year with its dominant cycle phase, using the history from Chapters 1 and 2.
Step 2: write down what the textbook clock predicts for that phase.
Step 3: compare each sector's return with the Nifty 50, and judge whether the prediction held, partly held, or failed.

body.text: These are price returns, which exclude dividends, so high-dividend sectors such as FMCG, energy, and PSU banks are slightly understated. Calendar years do not line up neatly with cycle phases, and the phase labels are assigned with hindsight. Treat the results as evidence, not proof.

children.text: The Raw Evidence

body.caption: Calendar year price returns, 2022 to 15 September 2026 (%)

children.text: Before testing anything, notice the spread. In 2023 alone, the gap between the best sector, Nifty Realty at +81.3%, and the Nifty 50 at +20.0% was more than 60 percentage points. In 2026 so far, Nifty Pharma is +15.2% while Nifty IT is -22.0%. Sector choice matters enormously, which is exactly why a framework for it is worth testing.
Test 1: The Slowdown of 2018 and 2019
The IL&FS defaults of September 2018 froze NBFC funding, auto sales slumped, and GDP growth slid to 3.9% in FY20. The clock predicts that cyclicals lag and defensives lead.

The cyclical half of the prediction held clearly: autos, metals, PSU banks, realty, and infrastructure all lagged badly. The defensive half did not. FMCG lagged the market slightly and pharma lost money. The real winners were high quality private financials and IT, businesses investors saw as safe for reasons the textbook does not capture: strong balance sheets during an NBFC crisis, and dollar earnings.
Test 2: The Contraction of 2020
The clock predicts defensives and health care outperform while lenders and rate sensitives lag.

Partly held. Pharma outperformed massively and banks lagged, just as predicted. But FMCG only matched the market, and IT, which the clock does not classify as defensive, was one of the biggest winners as the pandemic accelerated global digital spending. The shock itself decided the winners as much as the phase did.
Test 3: The Recovery of 2021
The clock predicts that rate sensitive, early cycle sectors lead: banks, autos, and real estate.

body.title: 2021: sector return minus Nifty 50 return (percentage points)

children.text: Partly held. Realty (+30.1 pp) and PSU banks (+20.3 pp) led as early cycle sectors should. But Nifty Bank lagged by 10.6 pp and autos lagged too, held back by lingering bad loan worries and a global semiconductor shortage. The biggest winners were metals, a textbook mid to late cycle sector, lifted by a global commodity boom, and IT, still riding global digital demand.
Test 4: The Expansion and Hiking Cycle of 2022 and 2023

The RBI raised the repo rate by 250 bps, government capex surged, and credit growth accelerated. The clock predicts capex, commodity, and energy sectors lead; Lesson 2.3 adds that banks benefit early in a hiking cycle as loan yields reprice upwards.

Largely held. PSU banks, energy, infrastructure, and metals all beat the market, and IT, hit by a global tech slowdown, lagged badly. Three surprises: autos surged as chip supply normalised and pent-up demand was released; realty beat the market despite rising rates, driven by the housing cycle described in Lesson 3.2; and FMCG also outperformed, helped as input cost inflation eased through 2023.
Test 5: The Soft Patch and Easing of 2025
Growth softened, earnings slowed, and the RBI cut rates by 125 bps. The clock predicts rate sensitives rally on cuts, while defensives protect in a softer economy.

Partly held, and it split cleanly. Banks and autos rallied as predicted, with autos also boosted by the GST 2.0 cuts. But real estate, the most rate sensitive sector of all, fell sharply as housing volumes declined, and the defensives failed to defend: FMCG and pharma both lost money while the market rose.
Test 6: The 2026 Crude Shock, So Far

Through 15 September 2026, Brent crude spiked above US$100, CPI inflation rose, bond yields climbed, and the Nifty 50 fell. On the Investment Clock, that looks like overheat sliding towards stagflation, which predicts commodities and energy outperform while defensive growth sectors like FMCG get squeezed by input costs.

body.title: 2026 to 15 September: sector return minus Nifty 50 return (percentage points)

children.text: Mostly holding, with the test still in progress. Metals and energy have beaten a falling market, and FMCG has lagged it, both as the clock predicts. Pharma, the top performer at +15.2%, fits the defensive role. But IT, at -22.0%, shows once more that it follows global tech spending and US policy rather than the Indian cycle.
The Scorecard

body.text: The pattern across all six tests is consistent. The broad direction of the clock, cyclicals versus defensives, usually held. Individual sector calls failed often, and almost always for a reason specific to that sector or to India: an NBFC crisis, a pandemic, a chip shortage, a GST change, a housing cycle, or global tech spending. The clock is a useful first filter, not a sector-picking machine. Lesson 4.3 explains why India breaks the textbook so often.

body.title: Go deeper: limitations of this test

children.text: Small sample. Six tests over nine years cannot establish statistical significance. Each Indian phase appears only once or twice.
Calendar years blur phases. A recovery that starts in mid 2020 is split across two calendar years. Monthly or quarterly data would be sharper.
Hindsight labels. The phases were assigned knowing what happened. In real time, as Chapter 2 showed, the phase is uncertain.
Markets lead. Because stocks discount the future, sector moves often happen before the phase they are "supposed" to belong to, so a strictly same-year test understates the clock.
Index composition changes. Sectoral indices add and drop stocks, and a few large companies can dominate an index's return.
Price returns only. Dividends are excluded, which penalises higher-yield sectors.
Practice

body.title: Compound Two Years
body.prompt: The Nifty 50 returned +3.2% in 2018 and +12.0% in 2019. What was its compounded two-year return? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: (1 + 0.032) x (1 + 0.120) minus 1 gives about 15.6%. Adding the two returns would give 15.2%, which slightly overstates it. Compounding matters more the larger the returns: for the Nifty PSU Bank over 2022 and 2023, simple addition understates the true gain by more than 20 percentage points.

body.title: Measure Relative Performance
body.prompt: In 2022, Nifty PSU Bank returned +70.7% and the Nifty 50 returned +4.3%. By how many percentage points did PSU banks outperform?
body.explanation: +70.7 minus +4.3 is about 66.3 percentage points. That was the first year of the RBI hiking cycle, when banks with fast-repricing loans and cleaned-up balance sheets benefited, consistent with Lesson 2.3.

body.title: Where the Recovery Test Failed
body.question: In the 2021 recovery, which textbook early cycle prediction failed most clearly on NSE data?
options: Nifty PSU Bank outperforming the Nifty 50
body.explanation: Nifty Bank returned +13.5% against the Nifty 50's +24.1%, lagging by about 10.6 pp, even though banks are the classic early cycle leader. Realty and PSU banks did outperform as predicted. Metals did not underperform at all; they were the best performer of the year, and the clock would not have predicted a mid to late cycle sector leading a recovery.

body.title: Name the Unit
body.textWithBlank: A sector that returns 25% in a year when the Nifty 50 returns 10% has outperformed by 15 percentage ___.
body.explanation: The difference between two percentage returns is measured in percentage points, not percent. Outperforming by 15 percentage points is not the same as returning 15% more than the market; 25% is 150% more than 10%.

body.title: Using an Imperfect Clock
body.scenario: A friend reviews these tests and concludes: "The clock only fully worked twice in six tests. Sector rotation is useless, so I will just hold an index fund." Another friend concludes the opposite: "Direction was right in every test, so I will rotate my whole portfolio into whichever sectors the clock favours each year."
body.prompt: What is the more balanced conclusion from this evidence, and how would you use the clock in practice?
body.modelAnswer: Both friends overreach. The evidence says the broad cyclical versus defensive tilt was usually pointing the right way, which makes the clock a useful first filter, but specific sector calls failed often because of sector-specific and India-specific drivers such as the NBFC crisis, the pandemic, chip shortages, GST changes, and global tech spending. So the index fund approach is perfectly reasonable as a core, and full-portfolio rotation is far too aggressive for a signal this noisy. A balanced use is to keep a diversified core, use the clock to form hypotheses about which sectors may be favoured, then check each against sector-specific evidence such as earnings revisions, valuations, policy, and relative strength before making modest, sized tilts. Lesson 4.4 covers relative strength, and Chapter 5 covers position sizing.

body.text: This lesson analyses historical index data for educational purposes. Past sector performance and past relationships with the business cycle do not predict future returns. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy, sell, or overweight any sector or index.

points: Tested on NSE sectoral index data from 2018 to September 2026, the textbook clock largely held in 2 of 6 tests and partly held in the other 4
In the 2018 to 2019 slowdown, cyclicals lagged as predicted, but pharma fell and quality financials and IT led
In the 2021 recovery, realty and PSU banks led as predicted, but Nifty Bank lagged the Nifty 50 by about 10.6 pp while metals led
The 2022 to 2023 hiking and capex cycle came closest to the textbook, with PSU banks, energy, infrastructure, and metals outperforming and IT lagging
In 2025, banks and autos rallied on rate cuts, but realty fell 16.6% and the defensives failed to defend
So far in 2026, metals and energy have beaten a falling market while FMCG and IT lagged, consistent with a crude-driven late cycle
The clock's broad direction is useful as a first filter; individual sector calls need sector-specific and India-specific evidence
